title: ECC memory modules
summary: Memories in cars, servers and space systems protect every word with an **error-correcting code**. This topic treats ECC as a hardware module: encoder on the write path, check bits stored with the data, decoder with corrected/uncorrectable flags on the read path, plus overhead, scrubbing and error logging. It ends with a SECDED (39,32) encoder, decoder and ECC RAM in SystemVerilog.
objectives: Explain why memories need ECC and compare parity, SEC and SECDED.
Describe the ECC memory module and its ce / ue outputs.
Compute check bits and a syndrome by hand for a small Hamming code.
Compute the check-bit overhead for a word width.
Explain read-modify-write, bit interleaving and scrubbing.
Read and use a SECDED (39,32) encoder, decoder and ECC RAM in SystemVerilog.

blocks.md:
Memory cells are tiny. A particle from cosmic radiation or from the package can flip a bit (**soft error**); a weak cell can fail after years of use. Large memories — caches, DRAM, on-chip SRAM in cars and servers — therefore store a few extra **check bits** per word and correct errors on every read. This is **ECC** (error-correcting code).

Here we treat ECC as a **memory module** — what it contains, how it is connected and what its signals mean. The mathematics of the codes is covered in the *Error-Correcting Codes* training.

steps.title: Write
steps.md: The **encoder** computes 7 check bits from the 32 data bits. The memory stores the whole 39-bit **code word**.

steps.title: Clean read
steps.md: The **decoder** recomputes the check bits and compares: the **syndrome** is 0 — the data passes unchanged, no flag.

steps.title: One bit flipped
steps.md: The syndrome is not 0 and points to the flipped bit; the decoder inverts it and raises **ce** (corrected error).

steps.title: Two bits flipped
steps.md: The decoder sees an even number of errors with a non-zero syndrome: it cannot correct, it raises **ue** (uncorrectable error).

rows: count it; log the address; rewrite the word (scrubbing)
do not trust the data: interrupt, retry, reset or safe state
blocks.caption: Outputs of an ECC memory

blocks.md: The idea is easiest to see with only **4 data bits**. Number the bit positions of the code word 1, 2, 3 … in binary. Positions that are powers of two (1, 2, 4) hold **check bits**; the others hold **data bits**. Each check bit covers every position whose binary number has *its* bit set.

steps.title: Overall parity
steps.md: SECDED adds p0 = parity of all 7 bits = 0. The memory stores 8 bits: 0 | 0110011.

blocks.md: **Decoding** repeats the same parity checks on the word that comes back from memory. Each check that fails sets one bit of the **syndrome** — and the syndrome, read as a binary number, is the **position of the wrong bit**.

steps.title: Check s2
steps.md: Positions 2, 3, 6, 7: 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 1 — this group contains the error.

steps.title: Check s4
steps.md: Positions 4, 5, 6, 7: 0 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 1 — this group contains the error too.

steps.title: Correct
steps.md: Syndrome s4 s2 s1 = 110 = **6**. The overall parity is odd, so there is exactly one error: invert bit 6, raise ce.

steps.title: Two errors
steps.md: With bits 3 and 6 flipped the syndrome is 101 = 5 — a wrong position! The overall parity is **even**, which reveals two errors: no correction, raise ue.

rows: single error at position = syndrome → correct, ce = 1
the parity bit p0 itself flipped → data is fine, ce = 1
double error → do not correct, ue = 1
blocks.caption: How the SECDED decoder decides
In hardware: one XOR gate per check bit in the encoder; in the decoder XORs give the syndrome, a small decoder selects the bit to invert

blocks.title: The 32-bit version is the same idea
blocks.md: For 32 data bits there are 6 check bits (positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) and one overall parity bit. The constant masks M0 … M5 in the SystemVerilog below are exactly the rows of the coverage table: mask Mk marks the data bits whose position has bit k set.

blocks.caption: SECDED overhead — wide words are cheaper

blocks.md:
That is why server DRAM modules are **72 bits** wide (64 data + 8 check) and why ECC is computed over the widest practical word.

Two consequences for the design:

- **Partial writes become read-modify-write.** Writing one byte changes the check bits of the whole word, so the module must read the word, merge the byte, re-encode and write back.
- **The decoder is on the read path.** It adds a few gate levels of delay; fast memories often add a pipeline stage for it.

blocks.title: Interleaving
blocks.md: Bits of one code word can be placed in physically distant cells (**bit interleaving**), so a single particle that flips several neighbouring cells hits several *different* code words — each with only one error, which ECC can correct.

items.title: Error counters
items.md: Every corrected error increments a counter. A sudden increase means a memory is getting worse — the system can react before an uncorrectable error happens.

items.title: Scrubbing
items.md: A corrected error is only corrected in the **output**; the cell still holds the wrong bit. A **scrubber** reads every word in the background and writes the corrected value back, so single errors cannot accumulate into double errors.

items.title: Testing the ECC logic
items.md: MBIST tests the cells with the ECC bypassed and checks the encoder and decoder by writing code words with deliberately flipped bits — see *MBIST Architecture*, Topic 6.

items.title: How was it verified?
items.md: A testbench wrote a word, then flipped **every single bit** of the 39-bit code word (39 cases: all corrected, ce = 1) and **every pair of bits** (741 cases: all flagged, ue = 1).

items.title: What is missing for a product?
items.md: Byte writes (read-modify-write), a pipeline register after the decoder, error address logging, counters and a scrubber — good exercises for the ECC lab M5.

questions.text: How many check bits does SECDED need for 64 data bits?
What does ce = 1 mean on a read from an ECC memory?
options: One bit was wrong and has been corrected in dout

questions.text: The decoder raises ue. What should the system do?
options: Treat the data as invalid and report the error

questions.text: Why is scrubbing needed although the decoder corrects single errors?
options: The wrong bit stays in the cell; a second error in the same word would make it uncorrectable
The decoder cannot correct without it

questions.text: Why does a byte write into an ECC-protected 32-bit word need a read-modify-write?
options: The check bits depend on the whole word
Bytes cannot be stored in SRAM
ECC memories have no byte enables

questions.text: Why is ECC usually computed over wide words?
options: The relative overhead of check bits falls with the word width
It removes the need for a decoder

questions.text: Simple parity can correct one flipped bit.
4-bit Hamming code: data bits at positions 3, 5, 6, 7 are 0, 1, 1, 0. What is p1 (covers positions 1, 3, 5, 7)?
The decoder computes s4 s2 s1 = 011 and the overall parity is odd. What does it do?
options: Invert the bit at position 3 and raise ce

questions.text: The syndrome is not 0, but the overall parity is even. What happened?
options: Two bits flipped — uncorrectable, raise ue
